title: Extended Isolation Forest with feature sensitivities
summary: The paper addresses the lack of controllable feature sensitivity in isolation-based anomaly detection. It proposes the Anisotropic Isolation Forest (AIF), an EIF variant whose split hyperplanes have normals drawn from anisotropic Gaussian or Gaussian-mixture distributions, plus directional sensitivity measures. On the Diabetes dataset, AIF(A3) with increased Age/DPF sensitivity finds anomalies with significantly higher Age and DPF values than EIF (Table I p=0.01 and 0.05).

match_target.why: The user target hint names exactly this value; it is also the cheapest direct reproduction of the paper's central Diabetes sensitivity result: one EIF and one AIF(A3) forest plus a t-test on Age.

tolerance.why: Rule 3: the p-value is bounded in [0,1] and the anomaly sets are smaller than 2,000 examples; the paper prints p-values as fractions to two decimals, so the bounded-score band is 0.02.

requirements.stmt: Sample split normal vectors from N(0,A) (or a Gaussian mixture) for AIF; do not use isotropic N(0,I) for the AIF model.
requirements.quote: we consider the EIF constructed using hyperplanes whose normal vectors are sampled from anisotropic multivariate Gaussian distributions N(0, A)

requirements.stmt: Use the EIF baseline with A=I, i.e. normal vectors from N(0,I).
requirements.quote: Then AIF(I) reduces to the standard EIF and exhibits constant unit sensitivity in all directions

requirements.stmt: Build 500 trees per forest, each trained on a random subsample of 128 points.
requirements.quote: each consisting of 500 search trees, with each tree trained on a subsample of 128 randomly selected data points.

requirements.stmt: Label the top 10% anomaly scores within each model as anomalies and compare these sets.
requirements.quote: For each model, we mark as anomalies the data points whose anomaly scores fall within the top 10% of all scores produced by that model.

requirements.stmt: For AIF(A3), set A3 = 1/1000 diag(1000,1000,1,...,1), mapping the first two diagonal entries to Age and DPF.
requirements.quote: so that the features age and DPF are assigned greater sensitivity, while all other features retain standard sensitivity

requirements.stmt: Compute anomaly scores with s(x)=2^{-E(h(x))/c(n)}, c(n)=2H(n-1)-2(n-1)/n, and H(n)=ln(n)+0.5772156649.
requirements.quote: where E(h(x)) denotes the average path length of x across all trees, and c(n) is a normalization constant

requirements.stmt: Traverse trees using stored split normal and intercept, sending (x-p)'ω <= 0 left and > 0 right.
requirements.quote: During the scoring phase, a candidate observation is passed down each search tree in the forest.

requirements.stmt: Compare EIF versus AIF anomaly sets per feature with an independent-samples t-test on feature means; the target is Age.
requirements.quote: We compare the mean values of the features of the anomalies identified by the EIF and AIF(A3) using a t-test for independent samples.

requirements.stmt: Use Table I feature ordering Age, DPF, Pregnancies, Glucose, BloodPressure, SkinThickness, Insulin, BMI when mapping A's coordinates.
For AIF(A4), set A4 = diag(0.001,0.001,1,...,1) with Age and DPF as the first two entries.
requirements.quote: so that the features age and DPF are assigned lower sensitivity, while all other features retain standard sensitivity

requirements.stmt: For AIF(A5), set A5 = 1/100 diag(0.01,100,1,...,1): Age low, DPF high.
requirements.quote: the feature age is assigned a lower sensitivity, while the feature DPF is assigned a higher sensitivity
